title: Garuda's Questions About Death
hook: the eagle who freed his mother asks Vishnu about death
carry: the soul travels on, and the family's rites help
tomorrow: why would a family shape rice into balls after a death?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alarka's ring for the worst day, and your line: satsang, good company is the cure for clinging. Today, a different Purana, a harder subject, and a look back at the week.

When someone dies, a house goes quiet in its own way, and in some Hindu families a book is read aloud over the days that follow. It's the Garuda Purana, or the part of it about what happens after death. Some people hear it with comfort. Some find it frightening, and some have only heard the frightening parts secondhand. So before the passages themselves, the frame: who is asking, and why.
screen: `A QUIET HOUSE.` → `A BOOK READ ALOUD.` → `FIRST, WHO IS ASKING?`

segments.voice: Garuda is the great eagle, the bird Vishnu rides, and the Mahabharata tells how he came to it. His mother, Vinata, lost a wager with her sister Kadru about the color of a horse's tail, and Kadru's snake sons cheated to win it. So Vinata became a servant to the snakes, and the price of her freedom was amrita, the nectar of immortality, guarded by the gods. Garuda flew up, fought his way through, and carried it off without tasting a drop. Vishnu, pleased that he hadn't kept it for himself, made him his companion and his mount. So the son who fought to free his mother is the one who, in the Garuda Purana, asks Vishnu about death: where a person goes, and what the living can do. Many teachers hear the fit in that. The answers carry a teaching most Hindus share: death isn't the end of the self. The atman travels on, and the family's rites, in the days after a death and on the yearly remembrance, help it on its way. That's why some families read these passages aloud at home after a death. Readers differ on how to hear the harder parts: as description, as a moral picture, or mainly as a rite for the family. And today: grief can feel like there's nothing left to do. The tradition says there is. Love still has work. And the week behind us: Kandu's sandhya, Vyasa's sung name, Harishchandra's truth, the Goddess who binds and frees, Madalasa's lullaby, Alarka's good company.
screen: `VINATA, A SERVANT.` · `GARUDA BRINGS THE AMRITA, UNTASTED.` · `GARUDA ASKS. VISHNU ANSWERS.` · `THE ATMAN TRAVELS ON.` · `THE LIVING CAN STILL HELP.` · then, large: `LOVE STILL HAS WORK.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes keep a photo of those who've died, with a garland, and light a lamp or incense before it on remembrance days. Let someone you've lost, or someone you love, come gently to mind, only as much as feels right today. If you pray, say their name, and then a name of God, or Om shanti, peace, for them. If you don't pray, say their name out loud, and one thing they gave you.
The Garuda. The Purana shaped as Vishnu's answers to his eagle's questions, with a section on what comes after death.
Your line: the soul travels on, and the family's rites help. Garuda asked; the answer was, love still has work. A week closes here.

howItsDone: In some Hindu families, the Garuda Purana's passages on death are read aloud in the home in the days after a death, often by a priest; other families don't use it, or keep only some of its rites.
